course: Physics - Mechanics, Waves, Electromagnetism and Modern Physics
attribution: Original scope and sequence authored for the Luminfest Learning Harness, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: An algebra-based introduction to physics: measurement, motion and forces, energy and momentum, rotation and gravitation, oscillations and waves, fluids and thermodynamics, electricity and magnetism, optics, and the relativistic and quantum ideas that close the course.

concepts.title: SI Base Units and Derived Units
concepts.summary: Every mechanical quantity reduces to powers of the seven SI base units, so the newton is kg·m/s² and carries the dimensions of force rather than a new base unit.

concepts.title: Dimensional Consistency
concepts.summary: An equation is dimensionally consistent only when both sides carry the same base-unit powers; a mismatch proves the equation wrong, while a match does not prove it right.
prerequisites: SI Base Units and Derived Units

concepts.title: Significant Figures in Measurement
concepts.summary: The significant figures of a measurement record the digits the instrument actually resolves, so quoting 12.30 cm claims a precision that 12.3 cm does not, and a product keeps the fewest figures of its inputs.

concepts.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
concepts.summary: A scalar is fixed by magnitude alone while a vector needs magnitude and direction, which is why 5 m of distance and 5 m east of displacement describe different states.

concepts.title: Vector Components
concepts.summary: Any vector splits into perpendicular components of magnitude V cos θ and V sin θ, and those components add independently, so one two-dimensional problem becomes two one-dimensional problems.

concepts.title: Adding Vectors Tip to Tail
concepts.summary: Vectors add by placing them tip to tail, and the Pythagorean result applies only to perpendicular components; at any other angle the law of cosines gives the resultant.

concepts.title: Order-of-Magnitude Estimation
concepts.summary: A Fermi estimate multiplies rounded factors so their powers of ten add, which fixes a quantity to its nearest order of magnitude even when each factor is uncertain by a factor of a few.

concepts.title: Random and Systematic Uncertainty
concepts.summary: Averaging N independent readings shrinks random uncertainty as 1/√N, while systematic uncertainty survives averaging because it shifts every reading the same way.

concepts.title: Position, Displacement and Distance
concepts.summary: Displacement is the change in position and is zero over a closed path, while distance travelled is the path length and never decreases.

concepts.title: Average and Instantaneous Velocity
concepts.summary: Average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, while instantaneous velocity is the limit of that ratio as the interval shrinks and equals the slope of the tangent on a position graph.

concepts.title: Acceleration as the Rate of Change of Velocity
concepts.summary: Acceleration is the change of velocity per unit time, so a body accelerates whenever its velocity changes, including when only its direction changes at constant speed.

concepts.title: Reading a Position-Time Graph
concepts.summary: On a position-time graph the slope at a point is the instantaneous velocity, so a horizontal segment means rest and a curl means changing velocity.

concepts.title: Reading a Velocity-Time Graph
concepts.summary: On a velocity-time graph the slope gives acceleration and the area between the curve and the time axis gives displacement, with area below the axis counted as negative.

concepts.title: Constant-Acceleration Kinematics
concepts.summary: For constant acceleration v = v₀ + at and Δx = v₀t + ½at² follow from the definitions of velocity and acceleration, and both fail once the acceleration itself varies.

concepts.title: Free Fall Under Gravity
concepts.summary: Near Earth's surface a body in free fall accelerates downward at about 9.8 m/s² when air resistance is negligible, whatever its mass.

concepts.title: Terminal Velocity
concepts.summary: A falling body reaches terminal velocity when the upward drag equals its weight, after which its acceleration is zero and its speed stops increasing.

concepts.title: Projectile Motion as Two Independent Motions
concepts.summary: A projectile's horizontal velocity stays constant while its vertical motion accelerates at g, so the trajectory is a parabola and the flight time is set by the vertical component alone.

concepts.title: Range and Launch Angle
concepts.summary: For a fixed launch speed over level ground the range is greatest at 45°, and complementary angles such as 30° and 60° give the same range.
prerequisites: Projectile Motion as Two Independent Motions

concepts.title: Relative Velocity in Two Dimensions
concepts.summary: Velocities combine as vectors between frames, so a boat crossing a current must aim upstream of its intended path and its ground speed is the vector sum of boat and current.

concepts.title: Newton's First Law and Inertia
concepts.summary: A body keeps its velocity unless a net external force acts on it, so rest and constant velocity are the same dynamical state and no force is needed to sustain motion.

concepts.title: Newton's Second Law for a Single Body
concepts.summary: The vector sum of the external forces equals mass times acceleration, so a body accelerates along the net force and not at all perpendicular to it.

concepts.title: Free-Body Diagrams and Their Conventions
concepts.summary: A free-body diagram draws only the forces acting on one chosen body, with weight always vertical and a normal force always perpendicular to the contact surface.
prerequisites: Newton's Second Law for a Single Body

concepts.title: Weight versus Mass
concepts.summary: Weight is the gravitational force mg and changes with the local field, while mass measures the quantity of matter and is the same everywhere.

concepts.title: Normal Force
concepts.summary: The normal force takes whatever magnitude prevents interpenetration, so it equals mg only on level ground with no other vertical force acting.

concepts.title: Static and Kinetic Friction
concepts.summary: Kinetic friction has magnitude μ_k N and opposes sliding, while static friction adjusts up to μ_s N, so a block stays put until the applied force exceeds that limit.

concepts.title: Equilibrium and Zero Net Force
concepts.summary: A body in equilibrium has zero net force, so the force components along any two perpendicular axes each sum to zero.

concepts.title: Forces on an Inclined Plane
concepts.summary: On a frictionless incline of angle θ the weight component along the slope is mg sin θ and the normal force is mg cos θ, so the acceleration down the slope is g sin θ.

concepts.title: Connected Bodies and Tension
concepts.summary: Bodies joined by a taut string share one acceleration, and a massless string over a frictionless pulley transmits the same tension at both ends.

concepts.title: Centripetal Acceleration
concepts.summary: A body moving on a circle of radius r at speed v accelerates toward the centre with magnitude v²/r even when its speed is constant.

concepts.title: Centripetal Force Is a Net Force
concepts.summary: The centripetal force is not an extra interaction but the radial part of the net force, supplied by tension, gravity, friction or a normal force depending on the situation.

concepts.title: Minimum Speed at the Top of a Loop
concepts.summary: At the top of a vertical loop the normal force vanishes at the minimum speed v = √(gr), so gravity alone supplies the centripetal force and any slower body leaves the track.
prerequisites: Centripetal Force Is a Net Force

concepts.title: Work Done by a Constant Force
concepts.summary: Work equals F d cos θ, so a force perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal force on level ground, does zero work.

concepts.title: Power as the Rate of Energy Transfer
concepts.summary: Power is work per unit time, equal to F v cos θ, so a given power lifts a doubled load at half the speed.
prerequisites: Work Done by a Constant Force

concepts.title: The Work-Energy Theorem
concepts.summary: The net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, and the statement holds even when the force varies along the path.
prerequisites: Power as the Rate of Energy Transfer

concepts.title: Kinetic Energy
concepts.summary: Kinetic energy is ½mv², so doubling the speed quadruples it and the same braking force then needs four times the distance to stop.

concepts.title: Gravitational Potential Energy Near Earth
concepts.summary: Near the surface the gravitational potential energy of a mass is mgh measured from a chosen reference height, and only its change is physically meaningful.

concepts.title: Elastic Potential Energy
concepts.summary: A spring deformed by x stores ½kx², so the stored energy grows with the square of the deformation and is the same for stretch and compression.

concepts.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
concepts.summary: When only conservative forces do work the sum of kinetic and potential energy stays constant, so a falling body converts mgh into ½mv² exactly.

concepts.title: Work by Nonconservative Forces
concepts.summary: Friction and drag change the mechanical energy by exactly the negative of the work they do, and the difference appears as thermal energy rather than disappearing.

concepts.title: System Boundaries in Energy Accounting
concepts.summary: The chosen system boundary decides which energies count as internal and conserved and which appear as external work, so one process can be booked either way.

concepts.title: Linear Momentum
concepts.summary: Momentum is mv, a vector, so a light body moving fast can carry the same momentum as a heavy slow one.

concepts.title: The Impulse-Momentum Theorem
concepts.summary: Impulse equals the change in momentum, so stretching the contact time for a fixed impulse lowers the average force, which is how airbags and crumple zones protect occupants.

concepts.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
concepts.summary: When the net external force on a system is zero its total momentum is constant, because the internal forces of an interaction cancel in pairs.

concepts.title: Elastic versus Inelastic Collisions
concepts.summary: Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision; in a perfectly inelastic one the bodies move together afterwards and the largest energy compatible with momentum conservation is lost.

concepts.title: Two-Dimensional Collisions
concepts.summary: Momentum conservation applies to each component separately, so a two-dimensional collision gives two equations for one event.

concepts.title: Center of Mass of a System
concepts.summary: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted mean position, so a system's translational motion obeys Newton's second law as if its total mass were concentrated there.

concepts.title: Motion of the Center of Mass
concepts.summary: Internal forces cannot move the centre of mass, so after an explosion the fragments' centre of mass continues on the original trajectory.
prerequisites: Center of Mass of a System

concepts.title: Angular Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration
concepts.summary: Angular quantities obey the same kinematic equations as linear ones with θ, ω and α in place of x, v and a, and arc length is linked to angle by s = rθ.

concepts.title: Rolling Without Slipping
concepts.summary: A wheel rolling without slipping has v = ωr at its centre, travels 2πr per full turn, and its contact point is instantaneously at rest.

concepts.title: Torque about a Pivot
concepts.summary: Torque is r F sin θ about a chosen pivot, so the same force gives more torque at a longer lever arm and none when it points straight at the pivot.

concepts.title: Moment of Inertia
concepts.summary: Moment of inertia is Σmr², so it depends on how far the mass sits from the axis: a ring resists spinning more than a solid disc of the same mass.

concepts.title: The Parallel-Axis Theorem
concepts.summary: Moving the axis a distance d from the centre of mass adds md² to the moment of inertia, so rotation about an off-centre axis is always harder.

concepts.title: Rotational Form of Newton's Second Law
concepts.summary: Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration, so for a fixed torque a doubled moment of inertia halves the angular acceleration.

concepts.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
concepts.summary: A spinning body has ½Iω² of kinetic energy, so a rolling body splits its energy between translation ½mv² and rotation ½Iω².
prerequisites: Rotational Form of Newton's Second Law

concepts.title: Static Equilibrium of Extended Bodies
concepts.summary: An extended body is in equilibrium only when the net force is zero and the net torque about one pivot is zero, which is two conditions rather than one.

concepts.title: Angular Momentum
concepts.summary: Angular momentum is L = Iω for a rigid body and mvr sin θ for a particle, so the same particle has different angular momentum about different origins.

concepts.title: Conservation of Angular Momentum
concepts.summary: With zero net external torque the total angular momentum stays constant, so a skater who halves her moment of inertia doubles her spin rate.

concepts.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
concepts.summary: Every pair of masses attracts with force G m₁m₂/r², so doubling the separation cuts the force to a quarter and the force on each body is equal.

concepts.title: Gravitational Field Strength
concepts.summary: The gravitational field g = GM/r² is the force per unit mass, so it falls with altitude and differs between Earth, the Moon and Mars.

concepts.title: Potential Energy at Large Separations
concepts.summary: Far from a planet the potential energy is −GMm/r with zero taken at infinity, so it is negative everywhere and rises toward zero as r grows.

concepts.title: Escape Velocity
concepts.summary: The escape speed √(2GM/r) is the launch speed that makes total mechanical energy zero, so it depends on the planet's mass and radius but not on the projectile's mass.

concepts.title: Speed and Period of a Circular Orbit
concepts.summary: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius r moves at √(GM/r), so a higher orbit is slower and takes longer despite covering a longer path.

concepts.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
concepts.summary: A planet sweeps equal areas in equal times because its angular momentum about the Sun is conserved, and its period squared is proportional to the semi-major axis cubed.
prerequisites: Speed and Period of a Circular Orbit

concepts.title: Weightlessness in Orbit
concepts.summary: An astronaut and spacecraft in orbit fall together at g, so the normal force vanishes; apparent weightlessness is free fall, not the absence of gravity.

concepts.title: Restoring Force and Simple Harmonic Motion
concepts.summary: Motion is simple harmonic exactly when the restoring force is proportional and opposite to the displacement, F = −kx, which makes displacement a sine or cosine of time.

concepts.title: Amplitude, Period and Frequency
concepts.summary: Amplitude is the maximum displacement and, for SHM, does not affect the period; period is the time for one full cycle and frequency is its reciprocal.
prerequisites: Restoring Force and Simple Harmonic Motion

concepts.title: Describing SHM by Phase
concepts.summary: The displacement x = A cos(2πt/T) is fixed by amplitude and period alone, so a phase angle states where in the cycle the oscillator sits.

concepts.title: Period of a Mass on a Spring
concepts.summary: A mass on a spring oscillates with T = 2π√(m/k), so a stiffer spring shortens the period while a larger mass lengthens it.

concepts.title: The Simple Pendulum
concepts.summary: For small angles a pendulum's period is 2π√(L/g), independent of its bob mass and only approximately independent of amplitude.
prerequisites: Period of a Mass on a Spring

concepts.title: Energy Exchange in SHM
concepts.summary: An oscillator trades ½kx² of potential energy against ½mv² of kinetic energy, and the total ½kA² stays constant while no damping acts.

concepts.title: Damped Oscillations
concepts.summary: Damping removes energy each cycle so the amplitude decays, and for a drag force proportional to velocity that decay is exponential in time.

concepts.title: Resonance
concepts.summary: A driven oscillator reaches maximum amplitude when the driving frequency matches its natural frequency, and weaker damping gives a taller and narrower peak.

concepts.title: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
concepts.summary: In a transverse wave the displacement is perpendicular to the propagation and in a longitudinal wave it is parallel, which is why sound is a pressure wave and a wave on a string is not.

concepts.title: The Wave Equation v = fλ
concepts.summary: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength, so in a fixed medium a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength because the speed is set by the medium.

concepts.title: Reflection and Transmission at a Boundary
concepts.summary: At a boundary between media part of a wave reflects and part transmits, and a fixed end inverts the reflected pulse while a free end returns it upright.

concepts.title: Refraction and the Change of Speed
concepts.summary: A wave entering a slower medium bends toward the normal because its frequency is fixed by the source while its speed and wavelength both fall.
prerequisites: Reflection and Transmission at a Boundary

concepts.title: Diffraction Around Obstacles
concepts.summary: A wave bends around an obstacle and spreads after an aperture, and the spreading is pronounced only when the aperture is comparable to the wavelength.
prerequisites: Refraction and the Change of Speed

concepts.title: The Principle of Superposition
concepts.summary: The displacements of overlapping waves add algebraically at every point, so two crests give a doubled crest and a crest meeting a trough can cancel.

concepts.title: Constructive and Destructive Interference
concepts.summary: Two waves interfere constructively when their path difference is a whole number of wavelengths and destructively when it is an odd number of half wavelengths.

concepts.title: Standing Waves and Harmonics
concepts.summary: A standing wave forms where two identical waves travel in opposite directions, and a string fixed at both ends supports only wavelengths 2L/n.

concepts.title: Sound as a Pressure Wave
concepts.summary: Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave travelling at about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, and its speed rises with temperature because molecules collide more often.

concepts.title: Sound Intensity Level in Decibels
concepts.summary: Sound level is 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) decibels, so a tenfold rise in intensity adds 10 dB and a hundredfold rise adds 20 dB.

concepts.title: The Doppler Effect
concepts.summary: An observer hears a higher frequency when source and observer approach and a lower one when they recede, and the shift grows with their relative speed compared with the wave speed.

concepts.title: Density and Specific Gravity
concepts.summary: Density is mass per unit volume and specific gravity compares it with water, so a body whose specific gravity is below 1 floats in water.

concepts.title: Pressure in a Fluid
concepts.summary: Pressure is force per unit area acting perpendicular to a surface, and at a point in a static fluid it has the same value in every direction.

concepts.title: Pressure Variation with Depth
concepts.summary: In a static fluid the pressure at depth h is p₀ + ρgh, so about 10 m of water adds one atmosphere of gauge pressure.

concepts.title: Archimedes' Principle
concepts.summary: A submerged or floating body feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

concepts.title: Floating and Sinking Conditions
concepts.summary: A body floats when its average density is below the fluid's, and it then displaces exactly its own weight, so the submerged fraction equals the density ratio.

concepts.title: Pascal's Principle
concepts.summary: A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished, so a hydraulic press multiplies force by the ratio of piston areas while the pistons move inversely.

concepts.title: The Continuity Equation
concepts.summary: For an incompressible fluid the volume flow rate A v is constant along a pipe, so narrowing the pipe speeds the fluid up.

concepts.title: Bernoulli's Equation
concepts.summary: Along a streamline of steady, non-viscous, incompressible flow p + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant, so faster flow at the same height means lower pressure.

concepts.title: Temperature and Thermal Equilibrium
concepts.summary: Temperature is the quantity that decides the direction of heat flow, and two bodies in contact exchange no net energy only when their temperatures match.

concepts.title: Heat versus Internal Energy
concepts.summary: Heat is energy in transit because of a temperature difference, so a large cool body can hold more internal energy than a small hot one.

concepts.title: Thermal Expansion of Solids and Liquids
concepts.summary: A solid changes length by αL₀ΔT and volume by βV₀ΔT, so expansion scales with the original dimension and matters most in long structures.

concepts.title: Specific Heat Capacity
concepts.summary: The energy needed to change a temperature is mcΔT, so water's 4186 J/kg·K makes it a slow-warming coolant and a stable heat reservoir.

concepts.title: Latent Heat of Fusion and Vaporisation
concepts.summary: A phase change happens at constant temperature and absorbs Q = mL, so melting ice at 0 °C takes energy without raising its temperature at all.

concepts.title: Calorimetry and Heat Balance
concepts.summary: In a thermally isolated system the heat lost by the hot bodies equals the heat gained by the cold ones, and that balance fixes the final common temperature.
prerequisites: Latent Heat of Fusion and Vaporisation

concepts.title: The Ideal Gas Law
concepts.summary: For an ideal gas pV = nRT links pressure, volume and absolute temperature, so at fixed volume the pressure is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

concepts.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
concepts.summary: Pressure comes from molecular momentum transfer to the walls, and the mean translational kinetic energy 3/2 kT depends only on absolute temperature.

concepts.title: Molecular Speeds and Effusion
concepts.summary: Root-mean-square speed grows as √(T/M), so at one temperature a light gas moves faster and effuses faster than a heavy one.

concepts.title: The First Law of Thermodynamics
concepts.summary: The first law states ΔU = Q − W, so energy entering as heat either raises internal energy or leaves as work done by the system.

concepts.title: The Second Law and Entropy
concepts.summary: The second law states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, so heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold and no cyclic engine converts all its heat input into work.

concepts.title: Heat Engine Efficiency and the Carnot Limit
concepts.summary: A heat engine's efficiency is W/Q_H and cannot exceed 1 − T_C/T_H, the Carnot bound set by the absolute temperatures of its two reservoirs.

concepts.title: Electric Charge and Its Conservation
concepts.summary: Charge comes in two signs, is conserved in every process, and is quantised in units of 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.

concepts.title: Coulomb's Law
concepts.summary: Two point charges repel or attract with force k q₁q₂/r², so tripling their separation reduces the force to one ninth.

concepts.title: Charging by Conduction and Induction
concepts.summary: Conduction transfers charge by contact while induction redistributes it without contact, so a grounded object can be left with the opposite charge.

concepts.title: Electric Field of a Point Charge
concepts.summary: The field of a point charge is kq/r² directed away from positive charge and toward negative charge, defined as force per unit positive test charge.

concepts.title: Field Lines and Superposition
concepts.summary: Field lines begin on positive charge and end on negative, never cross, and the fields of several charges add as vectors at each point.
prerequisites: Electric Field of a Point Charge

concepts.title: Deflection of Charges in a Uniform Field
concepts.summary: A charge launched across a uniform field follows a parabola, because a constant electric force plays the role gravity plays for a projectile.

concepts.title: Electric Potential Energy of Two Charges
concepts.summary: The potential energy of two charges is k q₁q₂/r, so like charges pushed together store positive energy and unlike charges store negative energy.

concepts.title: Electric Potential and Voltage
concepts.summary: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge, kq/r for a point charge, and only potential differences are measured by a voltmeter.
prerequisites: Electric Potential Energy of Two Charges

concepts.title: Equipotentials and Field Direction
concepts.summary: Equipotential surfaces are everywhere perpendicular to field lines, so moving a charge along one at constant speed requires no work.

concepts.title: Conductors and Insulators
concepts.summary: Charge moves freely in a conductor, so in electrostatic equilibrium the field inside it is zero and excess charge sits on its surface, while an insulator holds charge in place.

concepts.title: Capacitance
concepts.summary: A capacitor stores charge Q = CV at a given potential difference, and a parallel-plate capacitor has C = ε₀A/d, so closer plates store more charge.

concepts.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
concepts.summary: A charged capacitor stores ½CV² of energy, and inserting a dielectric of constant κ raises its capacitance by the factor κ at the same voltage.

concepts.title: Electric Current
concepts.summary: Current is the rate of charge flow, I = ΔQ/Δt, measured in amperes, and conventional current points opposite to the drift of electrons.

concepts.title: Resistance and Resistivity
concepts.summary: Resistance is V/I, and for a uniform wire R = ρL/A, so doubling the length doubles it while doubling the cross-section halves it.

concepts.title: Ohmic and Non-ohmic Conductors
concepts.summary: A conductor is ohmic only when its resistance is independent of the applied voltage, which is why a filament lamp gives a curved current-voltage graph rather than a straight line.

concepts.title: Series Circuits
concepts.summary: In a series circuit the current is the same through every element and the voltages add, so the total resistance is the sum of the parts.

concepts.title: Parallel Circuits
concepts.summary: In a parallel circuit the voltage is the same across every branch and the currents add, so the total resistance is smaller than any single branch.

concepts.title: Equivalent Resistance of Networks
concepts.summary: Series and parallel rules reduce any resistor network to one equivalent resistance, which then fixes the total current drawn from the source.

concepts.title: Electric Power Dissipation
concepts.summary: A resistor converts P = IV = I²R = V²/R into thermal energy, so transmission losses fall with the square of the current when the same power is delivered at higher voltage.

concepts.title: Energy Consumption and the Kilowatt-hour
concepts.summary: Electrical energy is power multiplied by time, and one kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 MJ, which is the unit a domestic meter bills.

concepts.title: Kirchhoff's Junction and Loop Rules
concepts.summary: Charge conservation at a junction gives the current rule and energy conservation around a loop gives the voltage rule, which together solve networks that series-parallel reduction cannot.

concepts.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
concepts.summary: Capacitors combine oppositely to resistors: in parallel their capacitances add and in series their reciprocals add, because they share voltage or charge respectively.

concepts.title: RC Charging and the Time Constant
concepts.summary: A capacitor charging through a resistor reaches 63% of its final voltage after one time constant τ = RC, and is treated as fully charged after about five.

concepts.title: Magnetic Field Lines and Poles
concepts.summary: Magnetic field lines run from north to south outside a magnet, close on themselves, never cross, and no isolated magnetic pole has been observed.

concepts.title: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
concepts.summary: A charge moving in a magnetic field feels F = qvB sin θ perpendicular to both v and B, so the force does no work and only bends the path.

concepts.title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
concepts.summary: A straight wire carrying current I in a field B feels F = BIL sin θ, which is the principle behind motors and loudspeakers.
prerequisites: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

concepts.title: Field of a Long Straight Wire
concepts.summary: A long straight wire produces B = μ₀I/(2πr) circling it, so the field halves at twice the distance while the current sets its strength.

concepts.title: Solenoids and Electromagnets
concepts.summary: Inside a solenoid the field is B = μ₀nI and nearly uniform, so more turns per metre or more current strengthens an electromagnet in proportion.
prerequisites: Field of a Long Straight Wire

concepts.title: Torque on a Current Loop
concepts.summary: A current loop in a magnetic field feels torque τ = NIAB sin θ, which turns its normal into alignment with the field, as in a motor or an analogue meter.

concepts.title: Magnetic Flux
concepts.summary: Magnetic flux Φ = BA cos θ counts the field lines through an area, so tilting a loop reduces the flux and at 90° it is zero.

concepts.title: Faraday's Law of Induction
concepts.summary: The induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux, so a faster flux change or more turns in the coil gives a larger emf.

concepts.title: Lenz's Law
concepts.summary: An induced current flows in the direction whose own field opposes the change that produced it, which is why a magnet falling through a copper tube drops slowly.

concepts.title: Maxwell's Prediction of EM Waves
concepts.summary: A changing electric field induces a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field induces an electric one, so the pair sustains a wave travelling at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀).

concepts.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
concepts.summary: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma radiation differ only in frequency and wavelength, and all travel at c in vacuum.

concepts.title: The Speed of Light and the Index of Refraction
concepts.summary: Light travels at c in vacuum and at c/n in a medium of index n, so a larger index means a slower wave and a proportionally shorter wavelength.

concepts.title: Visible Light and Colour
concepts.summary: Visible light spans roughly 400 to 700 nm, and colour is set by frequency, so light keeps its colour on entering glass even though its wavelength and speed change.
prerequisites: The Speed of Light and the Index of Refraction

concepts.title: The Law of Reflection
concepts.summary: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, so a plane mirror places the image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

concepts.title: Snell's Law
concepts.summary: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ fixes the bending at an interface, so light entering an optically denser medium bends toward the normal.

concepts.title: Total Internal Reflection
concepts.summary: Total internal reflection needs light going from a denser to a less dense medium at an incidence angle above the critical angle sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, which is how optical fibres guide light.

concepts.title: The Thin Lens and Mirror Equation
concepts.summary: The equation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i locates an image, and a positive image distance means a real image that can be caught on a screen.

concepts.title: Magnification
concepts.summary: Magnification is m = −d_i/d_o, so a negative value means an inverted image and a magnitude above one means an enlarged one.
prerequisites: The Thin Lens and Mirror Equation

concepts.title: Converging and Diverging Elements
concepts.summary: A converging lens or concave mirror has positive focal length and can form real images, while a diverging element has negative focal length and forms only virtual, upright, reduced images.

concepts.title: Young's Double-Slit Interference
concepts.summary: Two slits separated by d give bright fringes where d sin θ = mλ, so the fringe spacing grows with wavelength and with the distance to the screen.

concepts.title: Single-Slit Diffraction
concepts.summary: A slit of width a gives minima at a sin θ = mλ, and its central maximum is twice as wide as each side maximum.

concepts.title: Thin-Film Interference
concepts.summary: A thin film shows constructive or destructive interference according to the path difference 2nt, together with any half-wavelength phase shift at the boundary.

concepts.title: The Postulates of Special Relativity
concepts.summary: Physics is the same in every inertial frame and light's vacuum speed is the same for every observer, which forces space and time intervals to depend on the frame.

concepts.title: Time Dilation and Length Contraction
concepts.summary: A clock moving relative to an observer runs slow by the factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), and a moving object is measured shorter along its motion by the same factor.

concepts.title: The Photon and Quantised Energy
concepts.summary: Light exchanges energy in photons of energy hf, so an ultraviolet photon carries more energy than an infrared one whatever the beam intensity.

concepts.title: The Photoelectric Effect
concepts.summary: Electrons are ejected only when the photon energy exceeds the work function, and the maximum kinetic energy is hf − φ, independent of intensity.

concepts.title: Wave-Particle Duality and the de Broglie Wavelength
concepts.summary: Every particle has wavelength λ = h/p, which is measurable for electrons but negligible for a thrown ball.

concepts.title: The Bohr Model of the Atom
concepts.summary: Electrons occupy discrete levels, and a photon carries exactly the level difference when an electron drops, which reproduces the hydrogen line spectrum.

concepts.title: Atomic Spectra and Element Identification
concepts.summary: Each element emits a unique set of lines because its level spacings are unique, which is how spectroscopy reads the composition of distant stars.
prerequisites: The Bohr Model of the Atom

concepts.title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
concepts.summary: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp, because Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 bounds the product of their uncertainties from below.

concepts.title: Nuclear Structure and the Strong Force
concepts.summary: A nucleus of Z protons and N neutrons is bound by the short-ranged strong force, which must beat the Coulomb repulsion that grows with Z.

concepts.title: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Decay
concepts.summary: Alpha decay removes two protons and two neutrons, beta decay turns a neutron into a proton, and gamma emission carries away energy without changing Z or A.
prerequisites: Nuclear Structure and the Strong Force

concepts.title: Half-Life and Activity
concepts.summary: Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay, so after n half-lives the fraction remaining is 2⁻ⁿ and the activity has fallen by the same factor.
